Cyberattackers are weaponizing internet-connected supermarket freezers across Europe, spiking temperatures to 122°F and risking mass food spoilage.🌐
Evidence: Hacked fridges, 50°C heat spikes, supply chain threats
#Aletheia #Cybersecurity #FoodSupply

The Verge reports that unauthorized actors are infiltrating IoT refrigeration systems in European supermarkets, raising serious alarms about food supply chain security.

Invisible threat actors are actively compromising critical infrastructure, exploiting weak IoT security to cause physical destruction, fires, and massive food spoilage.

Grocery stores across Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, and France reported hacked freezers reaching 50°C, following similar French and US military base incidents.

The Poison:
Convenience-driven IoT integration without robust isolation transforms everyday appliances into remote physical hazards and supply chain weapons.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Plane Error: Confusing IT convenience with physical security. The system prioritizes remote telemetry access over fundamental physical safety isolation.

Social Physics Analysis:
Manufacturers and retailers run smart selfish loops, trading infrastructure security for remote convenience while externalizing severe supply chain risks.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.

Promising smart retail connectivity collapses into active physical destruction.

The Unavoidable Truth: Connected IoT appliances without strict air-gapping are trivial targets for destructive remote cyberattacks.
The Unavoidable Lie: Smart supply chains are inherently secure against physical sabotage.

Alethekanon:

Grocery stores across Europe have been hit by another wave of suspected cyberattacks, reporting sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers. Major supermarket chains across Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, and Estonia were affected according to local reports shared by Bloomberg and Reuters.

One Ica Kvantum store in Sweden said on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked overnight, with temperatures remotely raised to 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit). In a statement to Business Insider, a spokesperson at Swedish supermarket chain Coop also confirmed that “unauthorized actors were able to access and tamper with the cooling systems at a small fraction of our stores.” Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said an “IT incident” was responsible for adjusting the temperature of refrigeration units in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg. The full scale of the incident has yet to be confirmed.

Many modern supermarket fridges and freezers are connected to the internet to support remote maintenance and system failure alerts, but the increasing number of these suspected hacks is raising concerns around how security flaws can impact food supply chains. This latest incident follows an apparent cyberattack that targeted hundreds of French supermarket refrigerators last month, with the resulting food spoilage estimated to be worth millions of Euros, along with a string of US military base freezer malfunctions also suspected to be the result of a cyberattack.
